strengths: Addresses a genuinely novel and underexplored inverse problem: recovering dynamic 3D muscle deformation directly from multi-view RGB surface observations, bridging surface-only parametric body models and inaccessible medical-imaging-based anatomical models.

Introduces SKIM, a carefully engineered multi-view RGB dataset with a custom ArUco marker suit providing dense, temporally coherent, subject-specific skin/muscle/bone correspondences — a useful resource for the community given the scarcity of dynamic in-vivo soft-tissue data.

The decoupled muscle/skin blendshape formulation with biomechanically motivated regularizers (smoothness, bending resistance, stretch, tangential sliding, volume preservation) is a reasonable and well-justified way to resolve the inherent disentanglement ambiguity between muscle bulging and skin sliding.
Reasonably thorough ablation studies (architecture choice, vector regularization, physical energy terms) that support the design decisions and show clear, interpretable trends.

Comparison against a kinematic LBS lower bound and a recent generalizable volumetric predictor (HIT) illustrates qualitative and quantitative advantages in tracking accuracy and anatomical plausibility (reduced interpenetration, better volume preservation).
Provides an interactive visualization tool and per-muscle querying capability, which is a nice practical contribution for downstream graphics applications.
weaknesses: No direct ground truth for actual internal muscle shape/volume during motion (e.g., dynamic MRI/CT) is used for validation; all anatomical plausibility claims rely on surface marker tracking and physics-inspired proxy metrics (volume preservation, intersection ratio), which cannot fully confirm that the recovered muscle deformations are anatomically correct rather than merely physically plausible.

The method is strictly person-specific and demonstrated on only five subjects, limiting insight into generalization, robustness to body-shape variation, and statistical significance of the reported improvements.

The initial internal anatomical template relies entirely on an existing heuristic volumetric fitting method [30]; errors or biases in this template initialization propagate directly into all downstream muscle predictions, and this dependency is only briefly acknowledged as a limitation rather than analyzed empirically.

The comparison against HIT may be somewhat unfair/out-of-distribution, since HIT is a generalizable, SMPL-based, single-pose implicit model not designed for this cross-topology, marker-driven dynamic tracking setting; a more tailored or additional baseline (e.g., a simple pose-dependent skin+muscle blendshape without the proposed priors, or a lightweight biomechanical simulator) would strengthen the comparison.

Even the full model retains a substantial 10.35% deep muscle-to-bone volume deviation, suggesting the volume-preservation objective is only partially satisfied for the innermost anatomical layer; this residual error is acknowledged but not deeply analyzed.

The marker-suit-based capture pipeline is costly and impractical for broader use, restricting immediate applicability outside controlled studio settings (though this is explicitly discussed as future work).

Method description is dense with many symbols and equations without an intuitive summary walkthrough, which could hinder reproducibility and reader comprehension despite deferring several implementation details to supplementary material.

strengths: Addresses a genuinely under-explored problem: inferring internal (muscle) deformation from surface/skin observations rather than the more common forward (anatomy-to-skin) direction, which is a meaningful gap relative to prior surface-only body models and static anatomical templates.

The SKIM dataset introduces a carefully engineered acquisition pipeline (ArUco marker suit, multi-view mocap, high-res scanner, canonical marker-to-muscle correspondence via ray casting) that could be a useful resource for future soft-tissue research if released.

The method's cascaded, decoupled blendshape formulation (separate muscle and skin residual layers) combined with a set of physically motivated regularizers (volume preservation, tangential sliding, bending resistance, stretch) is a reasonable and well-motivated way to disambiguate the ill-posed muscle/skin decomposition problem.
The ablation studies (network architecture, vector regularization, physical energies) are systematic and help clarify which components matter for tracking accuracy and volumetric plausibility.

Comparisons against a kinematic LBS lower bound and an existing volumetric estimator (HIT) illustrate qualitatively sensible failure modes (candy-wrapper collapse for LBS, generic-template misalignment/over-smoothing for HIT).
weaknesses: There is no ground-truth validation of the actual internal muscle deformation itself; the only supervision/evaluation signal is sparse surface marker displacement plus hand-crafted physics priors. The paper's central claim ("recovering muscle deformations") is therefore never directly verified against true muscle geometry (e.g., MRI/CT/FEM), so it is unclear whether the recovered 'muscle' shapes are anatomically correct or merely a visually plausible byproduct of the chosen regularization terms.

The model is trained and evaluated per-subject on only five subjects, with generalization tested only on unseen poses of the same individuals, not unseen subjects. This severely limits the claimed scalability and practical impact, and is only briefly acknowledged as a limitation rather than substantively addressed.

The proposed capture pipeline (120-camera mocap studio, separate 140-camera body scanner, custom marker suit, volumetric template fitting) is itself expensive and non-scalable, which is in tension with the paper's stated motivation of providing a "scalable and cost-effective" alternative to FEM simulation — the method still requires an elaborate one-time subject-specific capture and cannot operate from casual/consumer RGB video despite the introduction repeatedly emphasizing accessibility.

The quantitative comparison to HIT may be somewhat unfair/uninformative given the fundamental mismatch in setting (HIT is a generic cross-subject predictor from a single MRI-trained prior, evaluated here on a different mesh topology via barycentric remapping, and not fine-tuned per subject), making the large error gap less conclusively attributable to the proposed method's core contribution versus a domain/setup mismatch.

Residual tracking errors remain non-trivial even for the full model (e.g., P90 ~19mm, DRE up to 65mm for large deviations, ~10% muscle volume deviation at the M→B boundary), and the paper's own discussion concedes the deep muscle layer volume constraint is not well satisfied, undercutting the claim of achieving anatomically grounded, physically consistent results.

The writing contains redundancy (e.g., near-duplicate sentences explaining canonical-frame pose invariance in Sec. 4.2) and leaves several implementation and dataset details (suit design specifics, exact number of sequences/poses per subject, train/test split composition) deferred entirely to supplementary material, making it harder to fully assess reproducibility from the main text alone.

The related work table (Table 1) contains an unusual/uncited future-dated reference ([8], listed as 2026, 'Botsch, M.') used as a comparison point, which raises questions about citation practices and whether the comparison table accurately reflects publicly verifiable prior work.

strengths: Novel and well-motivated problem formulation: recovering dynamic 3D muscle deformation from multi-view RGB/surface observations, an inverse problem not previously tackled at this level of anatomical detail.

SKIM dataset is a valuable, carefully engineered contribution: custom ArUco marker suit, high-resolution multi-layer anatomy (skin/muscle/bone), marker tracking pipeline with occlusion handling, and canonical correspondence construction — a useful resource for future biomechanics/vision research.

Technically sound method design: decoupled muscle/skin blendshape layers with a comprehensive set of biomechanically-motivated regularizers (smoothness, bending resistance, stretch, tangential sliding, volume preservation) that directly address the inherent ill-posedness/ambiguity of disentangling muscle vs. skin deformation from sparse markers.

Reasonably thorough empirical validation given the fundamental lack of dynamic in-vivo volumetric ground truth: multiple complementary metrics (global tracking, dynamic region error, intersection ratio, volume preservation) and comparisons against a kinematic lower bound (LBS) and a representative learned volumetric baseline (HIT).

Extensive and informative ablations (architecture choice, vector regularization, physical energy terms) that clarify the contribution of each design choice and show that naive fitting without priors leads to degenerate/implausible solutions.

Practical downstream utility demonstrated via a real-time visualization tool enabling per-muscle inspection, and a clear pipeline for propagating deformations to individual high-resolution muscle meshes usable in standard graphics engines.
Honest discussion of limitations (dependence on volumetric fitting initialization, marker-suit requirement, subject-specificity) rather than overselling the approach.
weaknesses: The dataset comprises only 5 subjects, and the model is explicitly subject-specific; this substantially limits claims of generalizability and the broader applicability of SOMA as a 'parametric' model in the conventional sense (i.e., generalizing across identities).

There is no direct ground-truth for internal muscle volume/shape during motion (e.g., dynamic MRI); all anatomical plausibility claims rely on proxy metrics (sparse marker residuals, volume preservation, intersection ratios) rather than validated internal muscle geometry, which is an inherent but still significant evidence gap for the core claim of 'recovering muscle deformations'.

The comparison to HIT may be somewhat mismatched, since HIT is a static, generic-template implicit model not designed for dynamic subject-specific tracking from sparse markers; the paper could benefit from additional baselines closer in spirit to the proposed task (e.g., simplified FEM or projective-dynamics baselines) to better contextualize the improvement.

Despite framing the method as 'scalable and cost-effective,' the data acquisition pipeline requires an expensive multi-camera markerless mocap studio (120 cameras), a separate 140-camera 3D body scanner, and a custom marker suit — this is a significant barrier to reproducibility and broader adoption that somewhat undercuts the stated practical impact, though this is acknowledged as future work (markerless capture).

Residual muscle-to-bone volume error remains relatively high (10.35%) even in the full model, and the paper's explanation (a 'realistic physical compromise') is plausible but not independently verified against any ground truth, leaving open whether this reflects genuine anatomical behavior or a modeling limitation.

The initial anatomical template relies on an existing volumetric fitting method [30], so errors or biases in that method propagate directly into SOMA's supervision signal and are not quantified independently in this work.

strengths: Novel and well-motivated problem formulation: inferring dynamic, pose-dependent internal muscle deformation from external surface observations, filling a clear gap between purely surface-based parametric body models and expensive/static FEM or MRI-based anatomical models.

Introduces SKIM, a new multi-view RGB dataset with a custom dense ArUco marker suit, high-resolution individualized skin/muscle/bone templates, and temporally coherent ground-truth marker trajectories for 5 subjects performing resistance-training motions; this is a useful resource independent of the downstream algorithm's performance.

The method (decoupled non-linear blendshapes for muscle and skin layers) is combined with a thoughtful set of biomechanically-inspired regularizers (smoothness, bending, stretch, tangential sliding, volume preservation) that are individually ablated (Tables 3-4), showing each term's contribution to anatomical plausibility and tracking accuracy.

Reasonably comprehensive evaluation protocol using proxy metrics (global tracking error, dynamic region error, intersection ratio, volume preservation) given the impossibility of acquiring in-vivo dynamic volumetric ground truth, and comparisons against a kinematic (LBS) lower bound and a state-of-the-art volumetric predictor (HIT).

Detailed and transparent supplementary material covering acquisition protocol, marker refinement/outlier filtering, network/training hyperparameters, prism-volume derivation, and marker visibility statistics, supporting reproducibility.

Provides a practical downstream mechanism (barycentric binding) to propagate learned boundary-layer deformations to individual high-resolution muscle meshes, plus an interactive visualization tool for per-muscle inspection.
weaknesses: The underlying volumetric muscle/bone templates are obtained via a heuristic, single-static-pose volumetric fitting method (not real MRI/CT), so the anatomical correctness of the muscle geometry itself is never independently verified; the paper's claim of being 'anatomically grounded' rests on this unverified initialization, which is acknowledged only briefly as a limitation.

No true dynamic volumetric (e.g., MRI-based) ground truth is available for validation; all quantitative metrics (tracking error, intersection ratio, volume preservation) are indirect surface/physics-inspired proxies rather than direct measures of muscle-shape accuracy, which somewhat limits the strength of the anatomical-plausibility claims.

The model is strictly subject-specific (5 subjects, small and demographically limited sample), with no demonstrated generalization across body shapes or unseen individuals; this restricts practical impact and is only discussed as future work.

Despite framing as 'vision-based' and 'from surface observations,' inference is actually pose-driven (skeletal pose θ is the network input); the dense multi-view RGB/marker suit is used only to generate training supervision, not as a direct runtime input. This could be clarified to avoid overstating the role of 'surface observations' at inference time.

The custom ArUco marker suit, 120-camera studio, and manual annotation tool required for data acquisition are resource-intensive, which is somewhat in tension with the abstract's claim of a 'scalable and cost-effective solution.'

The HIT baseline is arguably not designed for dynamic per-pose muscle bulging prediction, making the comparison somewhat unbalanced; no comparison to a physics-based (FEM) simulation baseline is provided to calibrate absolute accuracy, even though such comparison is acknowledged as expensive.

Quantitative results are reported in aggregate without per-subject breakdown, variance, or statistical significance, making it hard to assess robustness across the 5 subjects with differing body types.

strengths: Interesting and under-explored problem framing: inferring dynamic, subject-specific muscle deformation from multi-view RGB surface observations, bridging surface-only parametric body models and expensive FEM/biomechanical simulation.

Substantial data-collection effort: SKIM dataset with 5 subjects, a custom ArUco-embedded capture suit, 120-camera multi-view mocap, 140-camera static scanning, and layered (skin/muscle/bone/individual-muscle) canonical templates, released with code.

The biomechanically-inspired regularization suite (smoothness, bending, stretch, tangential sliding, volume preservation) is clearly motivated and formalized, including a non-trivial exact prism-volume derivation via Gauss-Legendre quadrature provided in the appendix.
Reasonably thorough ablations (network architecture, vector regularization, physical energy terms) that support the design choices for the loss and architecture.
Good overall clarity, detailed methodology description, and strong reproducibility effort through extensive supplementary material (capture protocol, parameters, data structure, metric definitions).
Honest limitations section acknowledging subject-specificity, dependence on an initial heuristic volumetric template, and the marker-suit requirement.
weaknesses: The central claim of 'recovering muscle deformation' is never validated against any actual muscle ground truth (e.g., MRI, ultrasound, ground-truth volumetric data); all markers lie on the skin, so the muscle-layer predictions are shaped almost entirely by hand-designed regularizers rather than observed data, making the decomposition between skin residual and muscle bulge an assumption rather than a verified recovery.

Evaluation relies substantially on physics-inspired proxy metrics (e.g., volume preservation) that are also directly optimized as training losses (λ_vol), creating a partially circular validation where the model is scored on criteria it was explicitly trained to satisfy.

The muscle template itself is obtained via a prior heuristic volumetric-fitting method (Komaritzan et al.), which the paper's own related-work section criticizes as limited in anatomical fidelity; this undermines the 'anatomically grounded' framing of the final muscle predictions, since errors in this initialization directly propagate.

Comparisons are between methods with fundamentally different data assumptions: SOMA leverages extensive subject-specific capture (45 min of multi-view video, custom suit) while the baseline HIT is a generic, static, single-scan predictor; the resulting large performance gap is unsurprising and not fully informative about SOMA's core algorithmic contribution versus its superior data access.

Marker coverage is notably low precisely during high-flexion / high-exertion poses (e.g., ~42% mean visibility for biceps/brachialis at peak curl flexion, ~55% coverage for push-ups), i.e., exactly the regimes where muscle deformation is most pronounced and most interesting to capture, weakening confidence in the learned deformations during the most relevant motion phases.

The dataset and models are limited to 5 subjects, all captured performing a fixed resistance-training protocol, and the method is explicitly subject-specific (no cross-subject generalization demonstrated), limiting the generality of both the dataset and the reported results.

The method's practical scalability is constrained by its reliance on a custom marker suit, large multi-camera mocap studio, and dense static body scanner, which are acknowledged as limitations but also substantially limit reproducibility and real-world applicability outside well-resourced labs.

strengths: Introduces a genuinely novel inverse problem: recovering dynamic, per-muscle soft-tissue deformation directly from multi-view RGB surface observations, addressing a clear gap between purely surface-based parametric body models and expensive/static internal-anatomy reconstructions.

SKIM dataset is a substantial engineering contribution: a custom dense ArUco-embedded suit, 120-camera markerless capture, careful multi-view triangulation with 2D/3D interpolation, temporal median filtering and motion-consensus outlier rejection, and a purpose-built annotation tool for resolving UV-seam marker artifacts. The acquisition and processing pipeline is documented in good detail (including in the supplementary), aiding reproducibility.

The decoupled muscle/skin blendshape formulation with biomechanically motivated regularizers (Laplacian smoothness, biharmonic bending, edge-length/stretch preservation, tangential-sliding, and canonical/posed volume preservation) is a sensible, well-motivated way to resolve the muscle-skin disentanglement ambiguity, and the formulation (including the closed-form prism volume via Gauss-Legendre quadrature) is mathematically clear.

The ablation study (architecture choices, vector regularization, physical energies) is reasonably thorough and supports the design decisions with quantitative evidence (Tables 3-4), rather than relying only on qualitative figures.

The paper is transparent about limitations (dependence on an initial heuristic volumetric template, subject-specificity, need for a marker suit, and unmodeled force/co-contraction effects at fixed joint angles), which appropriately scopes the claims.

Comparisons against a kinematic LBS lower bound and a state-of-the-art uncoupled volumetric predictor (HIT) provide useful, if imperfect, context for the proposed method's behavior, particularly the improvement in dynamic-region error and avoidance of layer interpenetration.
weaknesses: The internal muscle 'ground truth' is not derived from medical imaging (MRI/CT) but from a heuristic volumetric-fitting template (Komaritzan et al.), which the paper itself criticizes in related work as producing 'visually plausible but anatomically inaccurate' results. This makes the anatomical-accuracy claims for the muscle layer (as opposed to the marker-supervised skin residuals) largely unverified against any real anatomical reference, an important caveat given the paper's stated aim of moving 'from surface observations to muscle anatomy.'

Quantitative 'anatomical plausibility' metrics (volume preservation, intersection ratio) are self-referential to priors baked into the loss function, so strong performance on these partly reflects that the model was explicitly optimized against the same constraints used for evaluation, weakening the independence of the anatomical validation.

The method is trained and evaluated per-subject on only 5 individuals; there is no cross-subject generalization test, and the marker-suit acquisition setup is not a lightweight or widely accessible protocol despite claims of a 'scalable and cost-effective solution.'

In the main quantitative comparison (Table 2), the simple LBS baseline actually attains a lower mean tracking error (MPME) than SOMA, with SOMA's advantages concentrated in median/P90/DRE metrics; while explained via the 'candy-wrapper' rigid-collapse argument, this nuance slightly complicates the headline claim of uniformly improved tracking.

No perceptual or expert (e.g., biomechanist/clinician) evaluation is provided to corroborate that the predicted muscle bulging patterns are physiologically realistic beyond satisfying the imposed geometric priors; all evidence is either marker-tracking error or volume/intersection statistics.

The tight marker suit itself may introduce mechanical constraints on the skin (compression, marker rigidity) that could bias the observed 'ground-truth' surface residuals relative to unclothed skin motion, a possible confound that is not discussed.
